'''Robert James Silbey''' (October 19, 1940 – October 27, 2011) was an American theoretical chemist at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT). His research focused on the theory of electronic processes in [[Condensed matter physics|condensed phases]], including energy and [[electron transfer]], [[exciton]] dynamics, and the optical properties of molecular systems. He was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 2003.

==Early life and education==
Silbey was born in [[Brooklyn, New York]], the son of Sidney and Estelle Silbey.<ref name="NAS">{{cite book |last1=Berne |first1=Bruce J. |last2=Ceyer |first2=Sylvia T. |last3=Rice |first3=Stuart A. |title=Robert J. Silbey: Biographical Memoir |publisher=National Academy of Sciences |year=2014 |url=http://biographicalmemoirs.org/pdfs/Silbey_Robert.pdf}}</ref> He attended public schools in New York City and earned a bachelor's degree from [[Brooklyn College]] in 1961.<ref name="NAS" /> He completed his Ph.D. in chemistry at the [[University of Chicago]] in 1965.<ref name="NAS" />

After a postdoctoral appointment at the [[University of Wisconsin]] with [[Joseph O. Hirschfelder]], he joined the MIT faculty in 1966.<ref name="NAS" />

==Career and research==
Silbey spent his entire academic career at MIT, where he served as head of the Department of Chemistry from 1990 to 1995, director of the Center for Materials Science and Engineering from 1998 to 2000, and dean of the School of Science from 2000 to 2007.<ref name="NAS" /><ref name="MITobit">{{cite web |title=Robert Silbey, former MIT dean, dies at 71 |publisher=MIT News |year=2011 |url=https://news.mit.edu/2011/obit-silbey}}</ref>

His research addressed theoretical problems in condensed-phase chemistry, often in close interaction with experimental work.<ref name="AmerAcad">{{cite web |title=Robert J. Silbey |publisher=American Academy of Arts and Sciences |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/robert-j-silbey}}</ref> He made contributions to the theory of electronic excitation in molecular crystals, energy transfer processes, and the interaction of electronic and vibrational degrees of freedom in condensed systems.<ref name="NAS" />

Early in his career, Silbey developed quantum-mechanical treatments of excitations in molecular crystals, including analyses of exciton band structure and charge transport.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Silbey |first1=Robert |last2=Jortner |first2=Joshua |last3=Rice |first3=Stuart A. |last4=Vala |first4=Martin T., Jr. |title=Exchange effects on the electron and hole mobility in crystalline anthracene and naphthalene |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |year=1965 |volume=42 |issue=2 |pages=733–737 |doi=10.1063/1.1695999}}</ref> He later extended this work to exciton–phonon coupling and energy transfer in disordered systems and molecular aggregates.<ref name="NAS" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Grover |first1=M. K. |last2=Silbey |first2=Robert |title=Exciton–phonon interactions in molecular crystals |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |year=1970 |volume=52 |issue=4 |pages=2099–2108 |doi=10.1063/1.1673263}}</ref>

He also contributed to the theory of conjugated polymers, including calculations of electronic structure and optical properties, and analyses of nonlinear optical behavior in such materials.<ref name="NAS" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Brédas |first1=J. L. |last2=Chance |first2=R. R. |last3=Silbey |first3=Robert J. |last4=Nicolas |first4=G. |last5=Durand |first5=Ph. |title=A nonempirical effective Hamiltonian technique for polymers: Application to polyacetylene and polydiacetylene |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |year=1981 |volume=75 |pages=255–267 |doi=10.1063/1.441833}}</ref> His work on single-molecule spectroscopy addressed fluctuations, line shapes, and photon emission dynamics in condensed environments.<ref name="NAS" />

In later work, he studied energy and charge transfer in photosynthetic systems, including the role of coherence and environmental fluctuations in excitation transport.<ref name="NAS" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jang |first1=Seogjoo |last2=Newton |first2=Marshall D. |last3=Silbey |first3=Robert J. |title=Multichromophoric Förster resonance energy transfer |journal=Physical Review Letters |year=2004 |volume=92 |issue=21 |article-number=218301 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.92.218301 |pmid=15245322}}</ref>

==Teaching and administration==
Silbey was known at MIT for undergraduate and graduate teaching in physical chemistry.<ref name="NAS" /> He coauthored the textbook ''Physical Chemistry'' with [[Robert A. Alberty]] and [[Moungi Bawendi]], based on his lecture courses.<ref name="NAS" /><ref>{{cite book |last1=Silbey |first1=Robert J. |last2=Alberty |first2=Robert A. |last3=Bawendi |first3=Moungi G. |title=Physical Chemistry |edition=4th |publisher=Wiley |year=2004 |isbn=978-0-471-21504-2}}</ref>

As an administrator, he served as dean of the School of Science during a period that included new faculty initiatives and construction projects.<ref name="MITobit" /> He was also involved in efforts to address the status of women faculty in science at MIT.<ref name="NAS" />

==Honors and awards==
Silbey was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 2003.<ref>{{cite web |title=Robert J. Silbey |publisher=National Academy of Sciences |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/robert-j-silbey-truhxx/}}</ref> He was also a fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (elected 1991)<ref name="AmerAcad" />, the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]], and the [[American Physical Society]] (elected 1980).<ref name="NAS" />

His awards included the Max Planck Research Award and the J. O. Hirschfelder Prize in Theoretical Chemistry.<ref name="NAS" />
==Personal life==
Silbey was married to sociologist [[Susan Silbey]] and had two daughters.<ref name="NAS" /> He died on October 27, 2011, in Cambridge, Massachusetts.<ref name="MITobit" />
